display_name: Lafage, Côtes Catalanes Vieilles Vignes Tessellae
raw_content:
{
  "hook": "The Tessellae cuvée pulls fruit from scattered old-vine parcels across the Pyrénées-Orientales, where the Tramontane wind strips humidity and forces vines to drop their canopy. Jean-Marc Lafage ferments the Carignan and Grenache separately to preserve varietal tension, then blends in Syrah and Monastrell for structural backbone. The result is a direct, unapologetic expression of Roussillon’s hot climate and cool nights.",
  "wine_summary": "Domaine Lafage built its reputation on modernizing Roussillon without stripping the region’s rustic edge, and this bottling proves that approach works at the entry tier. Vieilles Vignes designations here mean vines pushing 50 to 70 years old, planted on deep colluvial fans that retain heat through the night and push sugar accumulation. The resulting wine carries the dark plum and iron signature of old-vine Syrah and Carignan, while the 14.5% alcohol reads as ripe warmth rather than heat because the blend leans on Monastrell’s natural acidity to anchor the finish.",
  "terroir_expression": "Côtes Catalanes sits where the eastern Pyrenees drop into the Mediterranean plain, leaving behind fractured gneiss, schist, and iron-rich clay. Schist fractures easily, forcing roots deep to find moisture, which translates directly to the dried thyme, cracked black pepper, and wet stone notes on the mid-palate. The region’s extreme diurnal shifts lock in acidity despite the high July temperatures, giving the wine a grip that stops the ripe fruit from turning flabby.",
  "vinification_summary": "Fermentation happens in temperature-controlled concrete tanks to preserve primary fruit while avoiding the oxygen exchange of oak. Lafage applies partial carbonic maceration to the Carignan, meaning whole clusters ferment in a sealed environment to build internal pressure and soften those naturally hard tannins before standard yeast fermentation takes over. The Syrah and Monastrell see extended maceration to extract color and structure, and the final blend rests briefly on fine lees to round out the mouthfeel without adding toast or vanilla.",
  "food_pairing": "Roast chicken thighs with smoked paprika and crispy potatoes need exactly this wine’s mid-palate weight and peppery Syrah edge to cut through the rendered fat. A classic Catalan botifarra sausage with white beans pulls out the wine’s iron and olive notes, creating a direct regional bridge. At the higher end, braised lamb shanks with preserved lemon and green olives work because the 14.5% alcohol stands up to the rich collagen while the wine’s herbal lift mirrors the citrus zest.",
  "comparable_wines": [
    "Jean-Luc Colombo Cornas — shares the Syrah-driven backbone but trades Roussillon’s schist for Rhône granite.",
    "Domaine Cazes Côtes Catalanes — mirrors the old-vine Carignan focus and Mediterranean spice profile at a similar price tier.",
    "Vignerons d’Estézargues Côtes du Rhône Villages — matches the GSM/Monastrell structure but reads softer on tannins due to deeper alluvial soils."
  ],
  "style_profile": "Medium-to-full-bodied dry red with firm tannic structure and savory Mediterranean herb character",
  "cellar_recommendation": "Store bottles horizontally at 12–14°C and keep them away from vibration. Drink within three to five years of release to catch the primary fruit, or hold until year eight for the Carignan’s savory depth to fully integrate.",
  "value_assessment": "$14.56 at LCBO prices this against mid-tier Côtes du Rhône and Languedoc blends, where most competitors sacrifice structure for easy-drinking sweetness. Tessellae outperforms them by delivering old-vine concentration and a clean finish that won’t fatigue the palate after two glasses. Buy it for the price-to-complexity ratio; you will not find schist-driven Carignan at this tier anywhere else on the shelf.",
  "market_position": "Restaurant wine directors stock this as a high-turnover house red because it bridges casual weeknight drinking and serious tasting notes without requiring decanting. The 14.5% ABV and approachable tannin profile make it a safe pour for mixed tables, while the Vieilles Vignes label gives sommeliers a concrete narrative to justify the pour price.",
  "insider_take": "Skip this if you expect oak-derived vanilla or jammy fruit; the wine deliberately avoids new wood to let the schist and old-vine tannins speak, which means it reads lean and peppery on first pour. It rewards a slight chill and ten minutes of breathing, but it’s not a decade-long cellar project — the Carignan’s earthy notes will peak around year five before the fruit fades.",
  "aging_potential_years": 8,
  "drinking_window_min_years": 1,
  "drinking_window_max_years": 8,
  "sensory": {
    "acidity": 3,
    "tannin": 4,
    "body": 4,
    "sweetness": 1,
    "alcohol": 4,
    "color_intensity": "deep",
    "aroma_intensity": "pronounced",
    "finish_length": "medium",
    "complexity": "moderate",
    "quality_level": "very_good"
  }
}
